hypothesis: The neuron selectively responds to high-contrast, diagonally oriented elongated structures, typically appearing as cylindrical tubes, metallic bands, or sharp linear strips. These features are defined by their luminous, light-colored surfaces—specifically bright white, silver, or light gray—set against a low-contrast, dark background of deep black, charcoal, or dark gray. A critical aspect of the activation is the presence of longitudinal texture or lighting, such as continuous specular highlights, parallel ridges, threads, or striations that run along the length of the object, emphasizing its three-dimensional or directional nature. The activating feature typically traverses the frame diagonally (most frequently from the upper-left to lower-right), occupying approximately 20–50% of the image surface and commanding the central visual field. The neuron remains invariant to the object’s specific identity—ranging from industrial tools and missile tubes to organic stems and fabrics—as long as the dominant diagonal geometry, cylindrical or band-like form, and strong light-on-dark contrast are preserved.
